[[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] businessman [[Bernie Moreno]] defeated [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] three-term incumbent [[Sherrod Brown]].{{cite news|last=Tobias|first=Andrew|title=Ohio's Sen. Sherrod Brown says he's running for reelection in 2024|url=https://www.cleveland.com/news/2022/09/ohios-sen-sherrod-brown-says-hes-running-for-reelection-in-2024.html|work=[[The Plain Dealer]]|date=September 13, 2022|access-date=September 16, 2022}}{{cite web |last1=Mutnick |first1=Ally |title=Trump-backed Moreno wins Ohio Senate primary |url=https://www.politico.com/news/2024/03/19/trump-backed-moreno-wins-ohio-senate-primary-00147945 |website=Politico |date=March 19, 2024 |access-date=March 20, 2024}} Primary elections took place on March 19, 2024.{{Cite web|title=2024 State Primary Election Dates|url=https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/2024-state-primary-election-dates|access-date=May 13, 2023|work=www.ncsl.org}} This was the first U.S. Senate race in Ohio where the incumbent was defeated since [[2006 United States Senate election in Ohio|2006]], when Brown defeated [[Mike DeWine]]. This race was one of two [[2024 United States Senate elections|2024 U.S. Senate races]] in which Democratic senators sought re-election in states where Republican [[Donald Trump]] won in both the [[2016 United States presidential election in Ohio|2016]] and [[2020 United States presidential election in Ohio|2020]] presidential elections (the other being [[2024 United States Senate election in Montana|Montana]]). This was the most expensive U.S. Senate election of 2024, with a record-breaking $483.4 million spent in total.{{Cite web |last=Mort |first=Ethan |date=December 4, 2024 |title=In Review '24: Ohio Senate General Election Saw a Record Breaking $483.4M |url=https://adimpact.com/blog/2024-ohio-senate-general-election/?utm_medium=email&_hsmi=338481034&utm_content=338481034&utm_source=hs_email |website=AdImpact}}{{Cite web|url=https://www.axios.com/2024/11/01/mcconnell-senate-leadership-fund-ohio-bernie-moreno-election-2024|title=McConnell's extreme tab on Ohio Senate race|date=November 1, 2024|first1=Hans|last1=Nichols|first2=Stef W.|last2=Kight|website=Axios}} Brown's reelection was considered essential for Democrats' chances to retain the Senate majority in 2024.{{cite web |last=Everett |first=Burgess |date=August 2, 2022 |title=GOP eyes 2024 payback for Manchin's Dems-only deal |url=https://www.politico.com/news/2022/08/02/manchin-republicans-reelection-00049135 |access-date=August 29, 2022 |work=[[Politico]]}} Moreno won 8 counties that Brown won in [[2018 United States Senate election in Ohio|2018]], all of them located in northern Ohio: [[Ashtabula County, Ohio|Ashtabula]], [[Erie County, Ohio|Erie]], [[Lake County, Ohio|Lake]], [[Mahoning County, Ohio|Mahoning]], [[Ottawa County, Ohio|Ottawa]], [[Portage County, Ohio|Portage]], [[Trumbull County, Ohio|Trumbull]], and [[Wood County, Ohio|Wood]]. His campaign was aided by Republican nominee [[Donald Trump]]'s 11.21% margin of victory in Ohio, helping secure an outright majority for [[Senate Republican Conference|Senate Republicans]] for the first time since 2021, with a net gain of four seats in the [[2024 United States Senate elections|2024 elections]]. Although Brown outperformed [[Kamala Harris]] in the [[2024 United States presidential election in Ohio|concurrent presidential election]] by 7.59 percentage points, it was not enough to win. Brown received about 120,000 more votes than Harris, while Moreno received about 320,000 fewer votes than Trump. Libertarian candidate Don Kissick received around 195,000 votes, approximately 3% of the vote. This was the first time since [[1954 United States Senate special election in Ohio|1954]] that a Republican defeated an incumbent Democrat senator in Ohio. Along with [[Bob Casey Jr.]] in [[2024 United States Senate election in Pennsylvania|Pennsylvania]] and [[Jon Tester]] in [[2024 United States Senate election in Montana|Montana]], Brown was one of three incumbent senators to lose re-election in 2024. Notably, all three were first elected in [[2006 United States Senate election in Ohio|2006]], defeating Republican incumbents, and won re-election in [[2012 United States Senate election in Ohio|2012]] and [[2018 United States Senate election in Ohio|2018]]. To date, this is Brown's second general election loss of his political career, having previously lost re-election in [[1990 Ohio Secretary of State election|1990]] as Ohio's Secretary of State to [[Bob Taft|Robert Taft]]. This wouldn't be Brown's final election of his political career; he would later run in the Senate again in [[2026 United States Senate special election in Ohio|2026]] for the other seat. Moreno's swearing in on January 3, 2025 gave Republicans control of both of Ohio's U.S. Senate seats for the first time since 2007. As Ohio's other U.S. senator, [[JD Vance]], was elected [[vice president of the United States]], Moreno became Ohio's senior senator upon Vance's resignation. {{TOC limit|3}} ==Background== After voting for [[Barack Obama]] in both the 2008 and 2012 presidential elections, Ohio has trended increasingly Republican in subsequent years and is now considered a [[Red states and blue states|red state]]. Republicans hold all statewide offices in addition to the majority in both chambers of the state legislature. Republicans also have majority of the state's [[United States House of Representatives|US House]] delegation.{{cn|date=February 2026}} [[Donald Trump]] won Ohio in [[2016 United States presidential election in Ohio|2016]] and again in [[2020 United States presidential election in Ohio|2020]] by 8 points both times.{{cn|date=February 2026}} Republican [[JD Vance]] defeated Democrat [[Tim Ryan (Ohio politician)|Tim Ryan]] in 2022 for [[2022 United States Senate election in Ohio|Ohio’s other U.S. Senate seat]] by slightly over 6 points.{{cite web|last=Dorman|first=John|title=Republican JD Vance has a narrow edge over Democratic Rep. Tim Ryan in the Ohio Senate race: poll|url=https://www.businessinsider.com/jd-vance-leads-ryan-ohio-senate-poll-dewine-whaley-2022-8|work=Business Insider|access-date=August 29, 2022}}{{cite news|url=https://www.cnbc.com/2022/11/08/ohio-senate-results-jd-vance-beats-tim-ryan-nbc-news-projects.html|work=[[CNBC]]|title=Republican J.D. Vance defeats Democrat Tim Ryan in Ohio Senate race, NBC News projects}} Brown was first elected in [[2006 United States Senate election in Ohio|2006]], defeating Senator [[Mike DeWine]] (who was subsequently elected [[Governor of Ohio|governor]]), and won re-election in [[2012 United States Senate election in Ohio|2012]] and [[2018 United States Senate election in Ohio|2018]]. If he had been reelected he would have been only the second Ohioan to be elected to the United States Senate by popular vote four times, the other being [[John Glenn]]. Abortion was a key issue of the election. Brown held a pro-choice stance, while Moreno held a pro life stance and won the support of [[Ohio Right to Life]]. Brown raised the issue frequently. Because of this, the topic of abortion made the news.{{#invoke:cite|web|url=https://www.beaconjournal.com/story/opinion/columns/2016/12/15/front-seat-view-ohio-s/10650754007/|title=Front-seat view of Ohio's space hero|date=December 15, 2016|website=Akron Beacon Journal|access-date=January 11, 2025}}{{Cite web|title=CNN.com - Elections 2006|url=https://www.cnn.com/ELECTION/2006/pages/results/states/OH/index.html|access-date=May 5, 2023|work=[[CNN]]}}{{Cite web|title=2012 Ohio Senate Results|url=https://www.politico.com/2012-election/results/senate/ohio/|access-date=May 5, 2023|work=[[Politico]]}}{{Cite news|date=January 18, 2019|title=Ohio U.S. Senate Election Results|work=[[The New York Times]]|url=https://www.nytimes.com/elections/results/ohio-senate |access-date=May 5, 2023|issn=0362-4331}} Initially, the seat was viewed by many to be a likely Democratic win, with some early polls showing Brown ahead, but Moreno attained a lead in the summer which grew through the duration of the campaign.{{Cite web|last=Yokley|first=Eli|date=January 11, 2023|title=Kyrsten Sinema Remains Among America's Most Unpopular Senators After Party Switch|url=https://morningconsult.com/2023/01/11/sinema-approval-rating-post-party-switch/|access-date=March 18, 2023|work=[[Morning Consult]]}} ==Democratic primary== ===Candidates=== ====Nominee==== * [[Sherrod Brown]], incumbent U.S. senator (2007–2025) ===Endorsements=== {{Endorsements box |title=Sherrod Brown |width=50m |list= '''U.S. senators''' * [[Mark Kelly]], [[Arizona]] (2020–present){{Cite web|url=https://www.politico.com/live-updates/2024/01/30/congress/senate-mark-kelly-battleground-2024-democrats-00138442|title=Mark Kelly isn't on the 2024 ballot.
